issues.description: The Procedure section describes the individual memory test as consisting of '20 open-ended questions,' but the Analysis Plan explicitly states 'the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.' These are mutually incompatible response formats. Open-ended questions require free recall and produce qualitative responses scored for content accuracy, while two-alternative forced-choice requires selecting between two pre-specified options and has completely different psychometric properties, scoring rules, and susceptibility to guessing. Additionally, within Section 3 itself, the opening sentence acknowledges a 'modification concerning applying open-ended questions,' which is then immediately contradicted by the statement that the forced-choice format will be used. This contradiction makes it impossible to determine what will actually be measured, fundamentally undermining the interpretability of all planned analyses.
issues.quote: The test will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details included in the movie [...] First we will examine the memory conformity effect using the procedure of Garry et al. (2008; also Ito et al., 2019), but with modification concerning applying open-ended questions in the individual memory test [...] In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.description: Section 2.3 asserts that 'discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced,' implying that which of the eight critical details are assigned to the discussed versus non-discussed conditions varies systematically across pairs or conditions to control for item-specific effects. However, Section 2.5 explicitly states that 'each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase,' with the example that 'all pairs will talk about Eric's cap color and his company logo.' These are logically incompatible: if every pair discusses identical items, no counterbalancing occurs. Without counterbalancing, any inherent memorability differences between the fixed set of discussed items and the fixed set of non-discussed items are completely confounded with the misinformation manipulation, potentially producing a spurious or inflated effect.
issues.quote: discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced [...] In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase. For example, all pairs will talk about Eric's cap color and his company logo.

issues.description: The study collects data from participants in pairs, but the planned two-factor ANOVA treats individual participants as the unit of analysis, violating the statistical assumption of independence. Each member of a pair participated in the same joint discussion, mutually influenced the other's responses, and was exposed to identical experimental conditions. Their post-discussion memory reports are therefore not independent observations. Analyzing non-independent observations as independent artificially inflates the effective sample size, reduces the error term, and produces anti-conservatively biased F-statistics and p-values. The appropriate approach would treat the dyad as the primary unit of analysis, use multilevel modeling with participants nested within pairs, or at minimum employ a within-dyad aggregation strategy. This issue affects all primary analyses and potentially invalidates the significance tests for both the main memory conformity effect and the intervention effects.
issues.quote: The results will be analyzed by means of a two-factor ANOVA, with one within-subjects factor with two levels (discussed vs. non-discussed items) and one between-subjects factor with four levels (three groups of methods of reducing memory conformity and the control group).

issues.description: The analysis plan first provides a nuanced, item-level operationalization of misinformation exposure, explicitly stating: 'if the partner provided an answer consistent with what the participant had seen...the situation will not be classified as misleading.' However, in the very next paragraph the plan contradicts this by stating: 'we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation.' The justification given ('the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version') confuses design intent with actual exposure. In cases where a partner guessed correctly, said 'don't know,' or the discussion did not result in misinformation transmission, participants would be scored as misinformation-exposed when they were not. This systematic misclassification attenuates the true misinformation effect, reduces statistical power, and creates a non-correspondence between the operationalization and the theoretical construct being measured.
issues.quote: However, if the partner provided an answer consistent with what the participant had seen, that is, 'white mug' (such a situation can happen, e.g., as a result of the partner's guessing), the situation will not be classified as misleading [...] we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version of events.

issues.description: The analysis plan specifies that all four derived indices (correct answers, misinformation-consistent answers, other answers, total answers) will be analyzed separately using ANOVA, with no mention of correction for multiple comparisons. With four simultaneous tests at α = .05, the familywise Type I error rate rises to approximately 19%. Additionally, the plan states follow-up pairwise comparisons will be conducted if the omnibus interaction is significant, but specifies neither which comparisons will be made nor what correction procedure will be applied. The power analysis separately notes 'comparisons among all groups and directional significance tests are assumed,' but no pre-specified hypotheses for each directional test are enumerated, nor is any alpha-level adjustment specified. Since this is a registered report, this level of underspecification in the analysis plan is especially problematic, as it preserves substantial post-hoc flexibility in reporting.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test's scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers [...] In the case of a significant main interaction, follow-up comparisons between pairs of groups will be performed.

issues.description: The exclusion criteria consist entirely of 'any technical problems during the experimental session,' with no pre-specified rules for several foreseeable situations: (1) participants who correctly identify the study's deception or the dual-film nature of the MORI technique before completing the memory test; (2) pairs where one member withdraws mid-session, rendering the other's data analytically unusable for the paired design; (3) participants who fail to comply with glasses-wearing instructions, potentially exposing them to both film versions; (4) pairs who fail to discuss any of the critical details during the collaborative recall phase; (5) participants who are non-native Polish speakers who may misunderstand instructions. The absence of pre-specified decision rules for these cases creates post-hoc analytic flexibility that could inflate false positive rates and makes the study impossible to replicate exactly.
issues.quote: We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.description: The study design pairs all participants into dyads for the MORI procedure, but the analysis plan provides no guidance on handling cases where one member of a pair drops out, is excluded, or produces invalid data after the joint experimental session. Because the misinformation each participant receives is wholly determined by their partner's statements during the discussion, the two members of a dyad are analytically inseparable. If one member is excluded (e.g., due to a technical problem, deception awareness, or voluntary withdrawal), the other member's data cannot be correctly scored for the primary outcome (discussed vs. non-discussed item accuracy), because the misinformation content itself would be unknown or confounded. With 120 pairs and no dropout plan, even modest attrition would systematically reduce the analyzable sample and potentially introduce bias if dropout is non-random.
issues.quote: The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs) [...] We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.description: The third experimental condition is termed 'Demonstration and motivation' consistently throughout the introduction, the design section, and the overview figure, but is relabeled as the 'DRM group' in the procedure section when describing the administration of that condition. This creates ambiguity about what the label refers to: is 'DRM group' shorthand for the full 'Demonstration and motivation' condition, or does it denote only participants receiving the DRM word-list task as a subset of that condition? In a registered report, labeling inconsistencies across sections suggest unclear procedural thinking and would impede post-study verification of adherence to the pre-registered protocol.
issues.quote: Participants in the DRM group will be given the DRM procedure with feedback, described above, which usually results in most of the participants falsely recalling a few of the critical lures.

issues.description: The authors assert that 'the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study' because the final memory test is individual. This claim is theoretically unjustified and overstated. Normative influence can persist in individual testing through multiple mechanisms: anticipated social evaluation (participants may anticipate comparing answers with their partner afterward), internalized consistency motivation (wanting to remain consistent with stated positions during discussion), and social desirability pressures that exist even without direct observation. The complete exclusion of normative influence as a possible mechanism is a strong theoretical claim that requires empirical support, not mere assertion. This matters because the entire theoretical architecture of the study, including the selection of informational-influence-targeting interventions, rests on this assumption. If normative influence is operative, the interventions may fail to reduce conformity not because they are theoretically wrong but because they target the wrong mechanism.
issues.quote: Given the fact that the individual memory test does not include any element of direct interpersonal pressure, we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.

issues.description: The power analysis for replicating the memory conformity effect uses a meta-analytic joint effect size derived from only two studies: Hedges' g = 1.92 (N = 55) and g = 0.38 (N = 74). These values differ by a factor of five and represent an extreme level of heterogeneity. Random effects modeling appropriately accounts for heterogeneity, but with only two studies a random-effects estimate is highly unstable and its confidence interval would be extremely wide. The resulting joint estimate of g = 1.13 (Cohen f ≈ 0.57) may be unreliable. Furthermore, the joint within-subjects correlation of r = 0.07 derived from these same two studies is implausibly low, suggesting near-zero relationship between discussed and non-discussed item accuracy. If the true correlation is higher, the within-subjects design confers greater efficiency than accounted for in the power calculation for the intervention interaction analysis, making it difficult to evaluate whether the planned sample of 240 is appropriately powered. The source of the dramatic heterogeneity between the two studies (possibly methodological differences in the Polish adaptation) is not investigated or explained.
issues.quote: The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges' g = 1.92, N = 55 (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges' g = 0.38, N = 74 (Kękuś et al., 2020)... Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13. This amounts to a Cohen f of about 0.57. The joint correlation of results in the discussed and non-discussed items in both studies available was 0.07.

issues.description: The validity of the MORI technique depends entirely on participants remaining unaware that they watched different film versions. The only post-hoc awareness assessment described is an open-ended question about 'the real purpose of the study,' which is inadequate as a manipulation check for two distinct reasons: (1) a participant could know they watched a different version without interpreting this as the 'purpose' of the study; (2) participants who realize the dual-film nature during or after the memory test—but not necessarily during discussion—are not identifiable. No direct post-session question explicitly asks whether participants noticed differences in their partner's account that could not be explained by differences in perception or memory. Without such a check, participants whose data are invalid due to deception awareness cannot be identified and appropriately handled, contaminating the sample.
issues.quote: Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.description: The Extended warning and Education about memory conditions are each described as 'approximately 7-minute' podcasts. The control condition involves a podcast of unspecified duration. The Demonstration and motivation condition includes a full DRM procedure (listening to word lists, writing down recalled words), feedback delivery, and a separate motivational podcast—a composite procedure that would substantially exceed seven minutes. This uncontrolled time-on-task variation across conditions confounds the intervention effect with the amount of time spent in a task: any difference in the Demonstration and motivation condition could be attributed to increased processing time, fatigue, or differential alertness rather than to the content of the intervention. A minimum requirement would be to equate the total duration of all four conditions.
issues.quote: The extended warning will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast [...] The training will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast [...] In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.description: The exploratory analysis plans to use DRM task performance as a predictor of MORI performance, implicitly treating both as indicators of the same latent construct (memory suggestibility). However, the DRM effect arises from automatic semantic spreading activation within a word-list paradigm with no social component, whereas memory conformity in the MORI paradigm arises from social informational influence on episodic event memory. These are mechanistically distinct phenomena. The correlation between susceptibility to the DRM false memory effect and susceptibility to social misinformation has not been established and has limited theoretical basis. Using an invalid proxy measure as a predictor introduces construct validity error and could produce null or misleading associations that are incorrectly interpreted as evidence about memory suggestibility as a unitary trait.
issues.quote: As an additional exploratory analysis, the results on the DRM procedure will be used as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique.

issues.description: Pair-level variables known from the literature to moderate memory conformity—including relationship familiarity, gender composition, perceived relative status, and interpersonal trust—are neither controlled nor measured. The manuscript acknowledges that age discrepancies can introduce confounds and restricts the age range accordingly, but ignores other well-documented dyad-level moderators. For example, the cited study by French et al. (2008) found higher conformity in couples than strangers, yet the study does not assess or control for pre-existing acquaintance between paired participants. Because participants are recruited via public advertisements and randomly paired, these uncontrolled variables become sources of unexplained within-group variance, reducing power to detect intervention effects and making it difficult to interpret null results.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet. The age of the participants will be restricted in order to avoid a situation in which a very young participant would discuss the original material with an elderly one, which would possibly activate some confounding factors (e.g., Gabbert et al., 2004).

issues.description: The collaborative recall procedure specifies that 'if the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented,' but the analysis plan provides no decision rule for how such items will be coded in the primary outcome analyses. Non-agreement items can be classified in at least three ways: as misinformation-exposed (if the participant heard the partner's incorrect answer even without consensus), as not misinformation-exposed (since no agreed answer was produced), or as missing/excluded. Each choice would produce different misinformation effect estimates. The omission of this pre-specified rule creates analytic flexibility that could inflate or deflate the apparent effect, and makes the study non-replicable.
issues.quote: If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented.

issues.description: Participants are seated together as pairs throughout all experimental phases. The fourth phase is described as an 'individual memory test,' but the manuscript does not specify whether participants are physically separated during this phase, whether visual barriers are used, whether the questionnaires are completed simultaneously or sequentially, or whether any instructions are given to prevent communication. If participants complete the so-called individual test while remaining co-seated and able to see or hear each other's responses, the test is not individual in any meaningful sense and would introduce additional misinformation contamination or conformity pressures during the critical measurement phase itself.
issues.quote: Immediately after the participants are done with the methods of reducing memory conformity (or the control condition), they will complete the individual memory test of the original material.

issues.description: The Integrative Framework for Memory and Performance (IMP; Blank, 1998) was developed for the classic misinformation paradigm in which post-event information is delivered impersonally via a written text or verbal narrative. The authors acknowledge this limitation but apply the framework to social memory conformity with only a brief analogical argument. The IMP's central construct—the 'consistency assumption'—refers to participants' belief that an experimenter-provided text is accurate. In memory conformity, the misinformation source is a live co-witness whose credibility, confidence, relationship to the participant, and social dynamics are all active. Research shows these factors moderate conformity in ways not captured by the IMP. The extension of the IMP to this paradigm is treated as established fact rather than as an explicit theoretical hypothesis, which overstates the theoretical grounding of the study.
issues.quote: The IMP was developed in the context of the classic misinformation paradigm, in which the post-event information is delivered impersonally. However, similar processes may apply to the memory conformity paradigm. When a participant, while discussing the original material with their partner, is hearing something different from their own recollection, they may assume that the partner is right and they themselves are wrong.

issues.description: The authors predict a specific ordered efficacy ranking: Demonstration and motivation > Extended warning > Education about memory. The reasoning for placing Extended warning above Education rests on the claim that Education 'only consists in providing theoretical knowledge but does not demonstrate any effects or motivate participants.' However, the Extended warning also consists largely of theoretical knowledge and verbal explanation; the key distinction—an enlightenment element revealing the deception—is a form of informational content, not a demonstration or motivational component. The ranked predictions are presented as derived hypotheses, but the theoretical basis for distinguishing the three interventions in terms of expected magnitude is no stronger than speculation. Presenting this as a directional hypothesis without stronger a priori grounding risks confirming a pattern post-hoc even if the true ordering differs.
issues.quote: we tentatively assume that the most effective technique in reducing the memory conformity effect will be Demonstration and motivation because it is based on demonstrating susceptibility to influence and includes an element of motivation to resist it. Moreover, on the basis of the fact that warning in general has produced inconsistent results in the context of undoing various kinds of suggestive influence, the Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory. We hypothesize so because Education about memory only consists in providing theoretical knowledge but does not demonstrate any effects or motivate participants.

issues.description: The manuscript opens and closes with strong forensic framing—erroneous testimonies as the leading cause of wrongful convictions, implications for justice systems—and the Demonstration and motivation intervention explicitly invokes court testimony. However, the sample consists of 16–35 year-olds recruited via media advertisements, representing a narrow, self-selected, predominantly young adult convenience sample. Real eyewitnesses span all age groups, include individuals with varying educational, cognitive, and psychological profiles, and are typically highly motivated by the actual stakes of testimony. The ecological validity of a voluntary laboratory study using a silent six-minute film of a staged theft as the 'witnessed event' is substantially limited relative to real eyewitness situations. No limitation section or discussion acknowledges these constraints on forensic generalizability.
issues.quote: erroneous testimonies continue to be the leading cause of incorrect court judgments [...] The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

issues.description: The Demonstration and motivation condition relies on four specific DRM word lists 'chosen on the basis of our previous research with this procedure' to produce a strong false memory demonstration. Only one of the four lists is provided as an example in the text. The four critical lure words used in the feedback ('doctor, window, sweet, thief') are disclosed, but the full associated word lists for window, sweet, and thief are not given anywhere in the manuscript. For a registered report, incomplete specification of materials critical to the manipulation prevents independent evaluation of whether the chosen lists will reliably produce the claimed false memory rates, and prevents exact replication of the procedure.
issues.quote: Four lists will be chosen which on the basis of our previous research with this procedure, produce the strongest effect [...] At this moment in this group, the experimenter will give the following information to the participants: 'Thank you for completing this memory task. Please take a look at your sheets now. See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief.'

issues.description: The reference list includes Condon, C. E., Ritchie, T. D., & Igou, E. R. (2015) on how dyadic reminiscence moderates familiarity, trust, and memory conformity—a directly relevant paper given the study's focus on dyadic memory conformity and the uncontrolled role of pair familiarity. This reference never appears in the body of the manuscript. Either it was omitted from the text in error (a reporting gap leaving out relevant moderation evidence) or was deleted from the text but left in the reference list. Either way, it represents an inconsistency and a potential gap in the literature review on factors that moderate memory conformity in dyads.
issues.quote: Condon, C. E., Ritchie, T. D., & Igou, E. R. (2015). How dyads reminiscence moderates the relations between familiarity, trust, and memory conformity. Social Psychology, 46(2), 65–75.

issues.description: The timeline section explicitly refers to a Stage 1 review process, indicating this is a registered report submission. However, the manuscript does not identify the journal, registry platform, or pre-registration repository where the study protocol will be or has been registered. For a registered report, the absence of this information makes it impossible for reviewers or readers to verify that the described analysis plan is indeed pre-registered, whether any deviations from a prior protocol have occurred, or whether the plan has been revised between submission versions. This is a basic transparency requirement for registered reports.
issues.quote: If the Stage 1 review is accepted, the resubmission should be completed no later than in 2023.
